summary: Kennebec River entrance light on a ten-acre Maine island: lit 1821, rebuilt 1855, automated 1960, a federal seabird refuge since 1973.

structures.note: Twenty feet, base to lantern centre (archive); present tower
Thirteen feet high at the 1842 inspection, as quoted by LighthouseFriends
Razed after the Coast Guard removed the buildings

access.note: The U.S. Lighthouse Society's archive lists the station as not open to the public. LighthouseFriends notes that the western end can be landed on in calm seas.

facts.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Maine Coastal Islands National Wildlife Refuge)

events.note: First tower, rubble masonry; Congress appropriated $10,500 for three Maine lights on 31 March 1821 (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Inspector I. W. P. Lewis described the tower as needing rebuilding (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Inspection: reflectors from the West Lighthouse at Cape Elizabeth installed here; new tower and lantern room recommended
Present brick tower, twenty feet tall, with a fifth-order Fresnel lens
Hurricane (dated 8 September 1869 by LighthouseFriends) blew down the pyramidal fog-bell tower; bell undamaged
Coal schooner dragging anchor under the lee of Pond Island; Hunnewell's Beach keeper and crew boarded and helped; revenue steamer Woodbury towed her into the river
New 1,200-pound bell hung in place of the corroded steel bell (LighthouseFriends)
Tug Battler with whaleback barge 202 caught in fog; barge anchor fetched up on the island; Hunniwells Beach crew assisted
Board fog-signal tests: the Pond Island keeper's view of how far the Seguin whistle carried
Fog signal changed 20 June 1895 from a blow every 8.5 seconds to a blow every 10 seconds
Keeper Ezra W. Morrison found dead after the lamp failed to reflect (Kennebec Journal, 17 June 1926)
Tern colony ended when gulls increased (LighthouseFriends)
Last resident keeper left on 11 September 1960 after the light was automated (LighthouseFriends); archive gives 1960
Refuge history: Coast Guard automated the station and removed the buildings
Transferred from the Coast Guard to the Fish and Wildlife Service; refuge established
Tern restoration programme begun by the Service, Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife and the National Audubon Society
First tern chick in over 60 years; ten pairs of common terns nested

corrections.why: The record gives the brick tower a build date of 1821. The brick tower was built in 1855 (archive year tower established 1855; LighthouseFriends). The 1821 tower was of rubble masonry.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Both dates are right. 1821 is the first light (archive year established; refuge: put in operation in 1821). 1855 is the present brick tower (archive year tower established). Wikidata's 1855 is the tower date.

notes_for_editor: (1) Automation date conflicts: archive and LighthouseFriends give 1960 (last keeper left 11 Sept 1960); the refuge says the Coast Guard automated it in 1963; Wikidata gives 1959 and Wikipedia's infobox 1963 (not cited). The story gives both. (2) Pre-1891 Lighthouse Board reports are not in the local corpus. The 1821 appropriation, 1823 petition, 1842 and 1850 inspections, 1869 hurricane and 1890 bell are second-hand from LighthouseFriends and should be checked against the Statutes at Large and the Board's reports. (3) Same-name trap: a second Pond Island with a light at Narraguagus Bay (Milbridge, Maine). The corpus hits for 'Pond Island' in 1894 and 1895 include both; this file uses only the Kennebec entries. A 1901 Ellsworth American item on a Pond Island keeper (Solomon Kelliher) refers to the Narraguagus island and is excluded. (4) Keeper dates: the archive's Isaac W. Morrison runs to 1903; LighthouseFriends to 1904. The 1926 Kennebec Journal says Ezra W. Morrison was keeper 29 years, which conflicts with the archive's 1904 start. (5) Hannah Gill appears only in the archive roster; no source read says more about her service. (6) The archive also lists 'Ira Winn' under 'Contractor'; not a keeper, so omitted. (7) The light's fifth-order lens status 'removed' is inferred from the present optic (250 mm). (8) The 1892 barge incident is dated 25 September from the certificate dated 26 September; the 'evening of the 25th' OCR reads '25t]h'. (9) The 1894 test date is not pinned (OCR reads '189S'); the story does not give one. (10) The 1895 entry is OCR 'of 8J seconds' (8½). (11) The 1902 notice's initials for the keeper are garbled in OCR, so the keeper is not named. (12) USLHS roster used as is; 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' is mapped to head keeper. (13) No new photos. (14) Verification 2026-10-27: the 1842 Lewis passage, the 1850 inspection and the 1869 hurricane are read through LighthouseFriends, and the story says so where the words are Lewis's. (15) The 1902 notice (Kennebec Journal, 26 April 1902, p. 6) reads in OCR as 'Mrs. R. W. Morrison, aged 70, wife of the keeper of Pond island light' and 'post 13 years' (read as past 13 years). The initials and the years need a check against the page image. The notice does not name the keeper, so the story and the keepers line do not link him to Isaac W. Morrison by name. (16) The 1884 schooner is named from the Life-Saving Service report: the schooner Electric Light, of Bath, Maine, bound from Baltimore with coal. The earlier 'Unnamed' entry was wrong. (17) LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open September through March with the tower closed; the archive says not open to the public. The story gives both and drops the landing invitation, since the island is a seabird refuge. (18) The 1895 fog-signal list is cited at scan page 44 (the Pond Island line appears on several scan pages of that volume); the printed page was not read. The 1894 Board page 325 is confirmed by the report's index. The 1892 Battler date (25 September) is confirmed by the Fort Popham certificate ('25th') and the 1892 Life-Saving table ('Sept. 25').
